newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Kuehbacher unsure EMU to start on time.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Kuehbacher unsure EMU to start on time.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said he is not sure European economic and monetary union (EMU) will start on time in 1999.

In an interview with the Berliner Zeitung released by the newspaper on Monday in advance of its Tuesday publication, Kuehbacher said Germany was unlikely to meet the fiscal criteria for EMU unless the government takes further measures.
Specifically, he said Germany is unlikely to meet the three percent deficit target unless Bonn passes a law to raise taxes or slash social spending.

Asked whether the euro would be launched in 1999 as planned, Kuehbacher said, "I am not so sure of that. In my estimation we will not meet the criteria unless the federal government takes further steps."

Asked if he doubted the Finance Ministry's projection that Germany's deficit would be 2.9 percent of gross domestic product this year, he said, "Yes, I do not see that we can reach three percent. Unless we pass another law and change the conditions that have been set down."
Kuehbacher said high unemployment, sluggish growth, job uncertainty, a high savings rate and weak consumer demand did not add up to a rosy scenario for meeting the EMU goals.

He said Finance Minister Theo Waigel's penchant for precision was his own undoing, as Germany would be judged by its own insistence on a strict application of the criteria. It would be hard to exclude Italy if Germany did not meet the guidelines, he said.

He also said he did not expect European countries to decide to delay EMU. Kuehbacher said he could understand if heads of government want EMU to start with a small core of countries including Germany, France and the countries that fulfil the criteria, so that the euro is as hard a currency as possible.

"The Maastricht Treaty must be interpreted the way it was intended: It must lead to a lasting consolidation of public sector budgets in EMU. That is why it was correct to conclude the stability pact. I do not know how else one could have done it."
